dimensions.gloss: How much of the work the AI/automation did, expressed as an ordered scale or typology running from none/assistive to full autonomy or generation.
dimensions.note: Groups several different tier/level frameworks (ASoP tiers, automation levels 0-5, clinical decision autonomy) with authorship-category scales (Fully Human to Predominantly AI-Generated) and the augmenting/displacing communicative-agency axis, because all describe the same underlying question of how much the AI did versus the human.

dimensions.gloss: Whether a given use of AI (as author, tool, or contributor) is allowed, prohibited, exempted, or otherwise governed as a policy stance, independent of how much detail must be disclosed.
variants: ai tools allowed in content generation
ai tools allowed in image generation
ai tools allowed in manuscript writing
basic tools for grammar, spelling, references do not require disclosure
dimensions.note: Combines explicit Yes/No allowed-fields, forbidden/permitted/encouraged task classifications, and three-way permitted/prohibited/disclosure models, since all record the same allow-or-forbid stance rather than the content of a disclosure.

dimensions.canonical_label: Task or activity AI was used for
dimensions.gloss: Which concrete task, activity, or content-type the AI was applied to (e.g. translation, image generation, literature review, feedback).
variants: ai use for coding or data analysis
ai use for image or table generation
ai use for writing or rewriting text
ai used in the conduct of research
dimensions.note: A broad basket drawn from many different schemes' task-type lists; grouped together because each label enumerates 'what was AI used for' rather than how much, whether allowed, or by whom.

dimensions.gloss: Which specific AI system, tool, model, or version was used, including structured identity records for the agent itself.
variants: characteristics of the llm models used

dimensions.canonical_label: Guidance on disclosure content and detail
dimensions.gloss: Advice or requirements about what a disclosure statement should specify and how much detail or granularity it should give (tool, task, location, technical vs intellectual use).
variants: be strategic about the level of detail.
clearer distinctions between ai assistance and ai generation
dimensions.note: Includes one concrete checklist field (which manuscript sections were AI-assisted) alongside prose guidance on disclosure detail, because both operationalize the same 'what/how much to say' axis.

dimensions.gloss: The duty or process of checking, verifying, or substantiating claims, citations, or facts produced with AI assistance.
variants: check drug claims with defined sources
dimensions.note: Folds in an advertising 'claim substantiation duty' (about product claims, not AI) because it records the same underlying obligation to verify claims made in a disclosed piece of content.

dimensions.gloss: Disclosure of the infrastructure, sources, and validation methods used to collect or annotate the underlying data.
Whether a data repository provides or enforces the metadata and community standards needed for citation and reuse.
Whether and how the produced software, code, or analysis artifacts were documented, licensed, and made available for reuse.
variants: category 1: develop software following standards and best practices
category 4: share software in a repository
dimensions.note: Merges a single scheme's five granular steps (dev standards, metadata, license, repository, registry) with generic 'script-sharing' and 'artifacts released' items from other schemes; the five steps are each arguably a distinct sub-axis, but all serve the same 'is the artifact shared and documented' question.

dimensions.gloss: Whether the human author, student, or clinician remains responsible and answerable for content produced with AI assistance.
variants: authors should retain final responsibility for their work
dimensions.note: Extends beyond 'author' to clinician accountability and to 'authorial mastery' (ability to defend one's own submission), since all three describe the human retaining answerability for AI-touched output.

dimensions.gloss: Structured identifying information about the human author(s), including name/affiliation metadata and professional background category.
dimensions.note: A stretch: 'author'/'authors' are bibliographic name fields while 'author category' records professional background (e.g. government official vs academic); grouped together as the only labels describing who the human author is, rather than what they did or are responsible for.

dimensions.gloss: A CRediT-style classification of the specific type of contribution a person made (e.g. funding, writing, conceptualization).
How strongly a disclosure or stated practice is required, on a scale from unnecessary/optional to mandatory or legally mandated.
variants: budget impact of the new technology
dimensions.note: Combines a legal document's 'assertiveness' scale (suggestion to legal mandate), a journal's mandatory-disclosure Yes/No field, and a health-technology-assessment publication-requirement field, since all three record the same strength-of-requirement axis in different domains.

dimensions.gloss: What functional role or job the AI was cast in within the interaction (e.g. learning assistant, case generator), and clarification of that role.
Whether mechanisms exist for a third party to review, explain, or reconstruct how an AI-assisted output was produced and checked.
dimensions.note: 'c-layer (semantic claims)' is a weaker fit — its example quote concerns graceful degradation when sources conflict rather than audit trails directly — but it appears alongside the other checkpoint-style labels in a governance framework.

dimensions.gloss: Organizational mechanisms for administering and reviewing AI policy, such as oversight boards and periodic policy review.
How adherence to a disclosure or AI-use policy is actually checked (or left unchecked), e.g. self-disclosure, instructor judgment, or explicit confirmation.
A type of vendor platform or technical layer used to automate AI compliance, as distinct from attestation itself.
Structured statements attached to a media asset describing its creation process, authorship, edits, and technology used.
dimensions.note: Same C2PA concept given in English and Dutch.

dimensions.gloss: An assertion that is supplemented with information about the entity confirming or endorsing it, distinct from the bare assertion itself.
dimensions.note: Kept separate from content-provenance-assertions because the source scheme explicitly distinguishes 'claims' (assertion plus confirming entity) from plain assertions.

dimensions.gloss: The technical mechanism (hard or soft binding) by which provenance metadata is bound to the content it describes.

dimensions.canonical_label: Mechanism of undisclosed influence on authorship
dimensions.gloss: A typology of the ways content or authorship is shaped by an unacknowledged party (ghostwriting, coercion, indirect steering) without full disclosure.
dimensions.note: Bundles three distinct typologies (ghost-management capture types, indirect-influence categories, coercive-authorship mechanisms) under one axis because each classifies a different form of hidden influence on who really produced the work.

dimensions.gloss: Who is able to access or interact with the AI system, from private personal use to public or institutional deployment.
How prominently a sponsoring brand is displayed or named within a piece of content (photo, header, hashtag, text).
variants: brand names mentioned in blog post

dimensions.canonical_label: Legal authentication standard for AI-related content
dimensions.gloss: The legal standard or procedural rule used to authenticate AI-related content as evidence, including who bears the burden of proof.
Whether the AI system was technically operational and accessible at the point it was needed.
Whether the human worker overseeing an AI-assisted process was actively engaged or attentive.

dimensions.canonical_label: Risk/severity if AI output is wrong
dimensions.gloss: The severity of harm or stakeholder risk that would result from an incorrect AI-supported output, used to tier review intensity.
A rated level of difficulty or complexity of the question or task given to the AI.
Whether a given AI operation is appropriate depending on the user's career stage or experience level.
Which communication channel or content format is chosen and how frequently it is used to reach an audience.

dimensions.canonical_label: Content of regulatory calls to action
dimensions.gloss: The specific obligations or actions a document calls on parties (e.g. model providers) to take.
Whether a document describes content-transparency mechanisms at the level of specific examples or as a broader general principle/hierarchy.
The technical mechanism for resolving a canonical identifier to a resource without requiring a public URI.
Whether a conflict-of-interest disclosure is present in the work.
Whether and how a bias or fairness analysis (e.g. defined subgroups) was planned for the AI-related work.
Whether calibration plots or confidence/prediction-interval reporting were provided for the model's outputs.
A specific named ethical principle (e.g. beneficence) invoked in the guidance.
The perceived credibility and trustworthiness (ethos) of content, rated high or low.
A named theme invoking AI-aware validity and ethical practice without a specific measurable field behind it.
dimensions.note: Kept separate from any 'transparency as virtue' bucket since no other label in this batch shares this exact vague framing.

dimensions.gloss: The degree to which an AI's presentation is deliberately calibrated to avoid inappropriate human-likeness.
The subject-matter field or research domain in which the AI was applied (e.g. clinical medicine).
A safeguard preventing perceived relevance of a source from being mistaken for genuine authority.
The degree of cognitive demand and evaluative judgement required of the human in an AI-assisted task.
Whether AI use was declared or not declared at all, as a binary presence flag rather than a description of content or detail.
dimensions.note: 'ai use disclosur' appears to be a truncated/typo'd label with no further quote context; paired with 'ai-related disclosure' (declared use vs declared non-use) as the closest matching axis.

dimensions.canonical_label: Which actor in the process used AI
dimensions.gloss: Which role in a workflow (e.g. authors versus reviewers/editors) is the one using AI.
variants: ai use by reviewers or editors

dimensions.gloss: A broad qualitative theme covering how AI use is governed in an educational setting, spanning permission rules, citation duties, and accountability together.
dimensions.note: Both are broad umbrella 'themes' from a qualitative coding scheme rather than single atomic fields; grouped together as the same higher-level theme rather than split across the narrower axes they touch on.

dimensions.gloss: A concrete strategy for redesigning assessment tasks in response to AI availability (e.g. staged submissions, oral defense, client-anchored briefs).
variants: assessment redesign to privilege documented reasoning
ai-assisted drafting plus in-class or oral verification
dimensions.note: These are design strategies rather than a measurable axis of a disclosure itself, but they consistently co-occur as a set in the education literature.

dimensions.gloss: How completely and accurately AI use or contributions are documented, from misleading/partial to adequate/traceable/complete.
An ordinal scale of which contributor (e.g. sole, primary, secondary, equal) receives credit relative to another.
dimensions.note: Related to but distinct from extent-of-ai-involvement: this axis ranks relative primacy between named contributors rather than how much an AI specifically did.

dimensions.gloss: A requirement that any AI-generated content used in one's work be appropriately cited.
Disclosure of known limitations of the AI tool itself, such as hallucination risk or model drift.
An umbrella label naming a set of integrity considerations (disclosure, verification, confidentiality, accountability) together rather than any one of them.
dimensions.note: A composite umbrella term rather than a single axis; kept as its own dimension instead of being split arbitrarily across the four sub-considerations it names.

dimensions.gloss: A named set of assessment rubric dimensions (e.g. concept mastery, evidence and verification) from a specific framework.
A bundled package of provenance-related components (payload, provenance graph, rights closure, trust profile, settlement policy) attached to a digital asset.
The type of public channel or trace (e.g. audit-report communication, narrative disclosure, market information) through which an undisclosed influence becomes visible.
Whether the scientific background, rationale, and context for evaluating an AI system is stated.

An umbrella label naming a bundle of computational-research reporting requirements (statistical transparency, code submission, data sharing, reproducibility, model parameters) together rather than any one of them.
dimensions.note: Overlaps with artifact-sharing-and-documentation-practice and statistical-calibration-reporting, but kept separate because it names the bundle itself rather than one specific requirement.
